newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysian PM at crest of high-tech wave.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysian PM at crest of high-tech wave.

text.p: If the adage of leading by example were applied to Malaysia's 21 million people, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad would be at the forefront of a net-surfing, video-conferencing, smart-card-using population.
The 71-year-old Mahathir loves gadgets and has embraced the use of computers and sophisticated communications in governance.

In December 1995, he was the first head of government to go live on the Internet, answering questions from people around the world. A month later, Mahathir, who has been prime minister since 1981, used the Net to hold a live dialogue with the leaders of Singapore and the Philippines.

He has also held several nationwide video conferencing "townhall" meetings, actively uses two computer terminals on his office desk and has personally canvassed support from high-tech luminaries for Malaysia's technology testbed, the Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC).
GOVERNING THROUGH CYBERSPACE
Malaysia's cabinet ministers have e-mail accounts, and Mahathir used video conferencing to keep in almost daily touch with his deputy Anwar Ibrahim while on a two-month absence from the country.
Asked if he was setting a new trend for governing in the future, Mahathir said the acceptance of high-technology is really coming from a more grassroots level.
"I think the people of Malaysia have risen to the challenge...they react very intelligently, to, for example, tele-conferencing. They come up with questions which are very valuable," he said.
"They seem to appreciate there will be changes in the way they live, the way they think, in their perception of things, and I think we have made a very early start."

Tengku Azzman Shariffadeen, chief executive officer of Malaysia Internet service provider MIMOS Bhd, told an Internet conference hosted in Malaysia in June: "Internet is doing a good job of revealing a new way of governance."
MULTIMEDIA CORRIDOR A PET PROJECT

Malaysia is looking to offer a number of new ways of expanding high-technology boundaries. Its most talked-about project is the MSC, a 15-by-50 kilometre (9-by-30 mile) high-tech, high-speed communications zone extending south from Malaysia's capital of Kuala Lumpur to its new international airport.

The MSC, which about 40 companies have said they will take part in, is seen as a "multimedia utopia" for developing multimedia products and services, said Leo Moggie, Malaysia's minister of energy, telecommunications and posts.
Malaysia has set up an international advisory panel that includes some of the biggest names in the computing world including Bill Gates of software behemoth Microsoft Corp .

Within the MSC, Malaysia is also planning the world's first intelligent city called Cyberjaya, where every home will have access to the Internet and all transactions will be done with smart cards. Cyberjaya will be spread over 7,000 hectares (17,300 acres) and eventually support a population of 240,000.
Part of the plans include a new high-tech federal capital called Putrajaya.
MAHATHIR DEPUTY ALSO TECHNO-FAN
Malaysia's techno-fans also include Anwar, Mahathir's deputy. "He loves to talk about the latest things he's downloaded from the Internet," said the chief executive of a Malaysian technology company.
The bookish Anwar, who delights in sprinkling elegant classical Malay words in his speeches, usually surfs for items on literature and book reviews.
High-technology industry officials in Malaysia have welcomed Mahathir's efforts.

"(It's) a very positive development when you have the leader actually showing the way. If it was only the tech guys pushing it, people would be more sceptical," said Ramesh Gopal, business development manager at U.S. networking firm Cisco Systems Inc , also an advisor company to the MSC.
Malaysia intends to wire-up all its schools, and envisions its high-tech projects as a key driver toward achieving developed status by the year 2020.

Unlike some draconian measures to restrict the Internet within Asia, notably Singapore, and despite its own laws that help keep the media in check, Mahathir has said repeatedly Malaysia will not censor the Internet.

Mahathir has advocated self-censorship for the majority Moslem population, despite fears expressed by religious leaders that some young people may spend time downloading pornography and getting influenced by "undesirable" western culture.
TECH REVOLUTION MOVING SLOWLY
For now, the high-tech revolution is starting up quietly, although there are trendy cybercafes springing up in cities where people can mix computer chat with cappuccinos.
Malaysia still has only two Internet service providers, and around 100,000 signed up on the Internet from its population of about 21 million. Computers are scarce in rural villages and many schools.
Singapore, with around three million people, has three Internet service providers. Japan, among the first Asian countries to get into cyberspace, has about 1,800.
"I think of it (technology projects) as a stretch goal," said Gopal of Cisco Systems. "This is a vision that can excite and drive people."
